clinicalPearls: Boomerang dysplasia is a perinatally lethal skeletal dysplasia caused by dominant, usually de novo, variants in FLNB (filamin B).
It is allelic with atelosteogenesis type I but sits at the more severe end of the spectrum, with more extensive failure of ossification.
The name derives from the boomerang-like radiographic shape of certain long bones, which appear bowed with a proximal or mid-shaft spike.
There is absent or severely deficient ossification of limb bones and some vertebrae, often with absent fibulae and other missing or profoundly hypoplastic bones.
A distinctive face with hypertelorism and a depressed nasal bridge is common, and omphalocele or encephalocele may occur.
Severe pulmonary hypoplasia due to a small thorax causes neonatal respiratory failure.
It is distinguished from atelosteogenesis type I chiefly by the degree of underossification and the pattern of absent bones.
Molecular confirmation of FLNB and genetic counselling are key; as disease is usually de novo, recurrence risk is generally low.
reference.pathophysiology: Boomerang dysplasia is caused by dominant, typically de novo, variants in FLNB, which encodes filamin B, a cytoskeletal actin-crosslinking protein essential for chondrocyte differentiation, vertebral segmentation and joint formation. It lies within the FLNB filaminopathy spectrum that also encompasses Larsen syndrome, atelosteogenesis types I and III, and spondylocarpotarsal synostosis. In boomerang dysplasia the mutant filamin B disrupts endochondral ossification so severely that many long bones and vertebrae fail to ossify, and some skeletal elements are absent altogether, giving the characteristic boomerang-shaped and non-ossified bones. The accompanying small thorax leads to lethal pulmonary hypoplasia.

reference.prognosis: Boomerang dysplasia is uniformly lethal in the perinatal period, typically from respiratory failure secondary to pulmonary hypoplasia.
pitfalls: Misclassifying it as atelosteogenesis type I given the spectrum overlap
Attributing it to recessive inheritance when it is dominant and usually de novo
Failing to send FLNB testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling
Confusing it with Piepkorn dysplasia on radiographs alone
management: Boomerang dysplasia is uniformly perinatally lethal, so management centres on accurate diagnosis and compassionate, non-curative care rather than active treatment
Antenatal recognition through ultrasound showing micromelia and absent ossification, supplemented by foetal MRI, to guide informed parental counselling and delivery planning
Confirmation by postnatal skeletal survey, chondro-osseous histology and FLNB molecular testing
Perinatal palliative and comfort care for the neonate, with respiratory failure from pulmonary hypoplasia the anticipated terminal event
Genetic counselling for the dominant, usually de novo FLNB variant, with prenatal or preimplantation testing offered in future pregnancies given the small recurrence risk from gonadal mosaicism
Bereavement support with multidisciplinary involvement of clinical genetics, perinatal medicine and palliative care
